analysis.one_liner: Requires Supreme Court justices to follow a written ethics code, disclose gifts, and face outside review of recusal decisions.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 35 senators, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2025 and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Supreme Court to adopt and publish a binding code of conduct for its justices, set up a process for filing and investigating ethics complaints against justices, and create a panel of outside judges to review recusal decisions. It would tighten gift rules and disclosure requirements for justices, require parties and outside groups that file briefs to disclose money or gifts connected to justices, and require public notice whenever a judge is disqualified from a case.
analysis.who_benefits: Members of the public who appear before federal courts. Ordinary people have no way today to force a Supreme Court justice off a case where they have a financial or personal tie, and there is no outside body that investigates ethics complaints against justices. The bill would give litigants a formal way to raise conflicts, force justices to disclose gifts and income from parties, and put outside judges in charge of reviewing disqualification decisions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to issue a code of conduct for its justices within 180 days, with public notice and comment, and to post the code and related ethics rules on its website in a searchable format [S2].

Creates a complaint system for misconduct allegations against justices, with a randomly selected panel of five circuit chief judges empowered to investigate, hold hearings, take sworn testimony, and issue subpoenas, and to publish findings when it does not dismiss a complaint [S2].

Requires a justice to step aside from cases involving parties that lobbied for or spent money supporting their appointment, or that gave the justice or their spouse or minor child income, gifts, or reimbursements within the previous six years [S2].

Lets parties file a motion to disqualify a justice and sends any contested motion to a reviewing panel for the Supreme Court that excludes the justice in question, instead of leaving the decision solely to the justice's own discretion [S2].

Requires parties and amici at the Supreme Court to disclose gifts, income, or reimbursements they or their lawyers provided to justices, and any spending supporting a justice's confirmation, and requires amicus briefs in all federal courts to disclose their major funders [S2].
Requires courts to publish on their websites every case in which a judge is disqualified, with an explanation of the specific reasons [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Supreme Court justices and federal judges bear the cost: binding ethics rules, mandatory disclosure of gifts and income, and the possibility of an outside panel forcing them off cases. Wealthy litigants and groups that spend heavily on Supreme Court advocacy would have to disclose their connections to justices. The Court and the Judicial Conference bear the administrative cost of writing and enforcing the rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Supreme Court justices and big litigants

drawbacks.text: The complaint process is largely run by the courts themselves: the Supreme Court writes its own code of conduct and the review of Supreme Court recusal decisions is done by the other eight justices, so the bill does not create a fully independent enforcer [S2].

Recusal motions can be filed by any party with an affidavit, and the bill requires the proceeding to be stayed until the motion is decided, which critics argue could let litigants delay or remove judges from cases through strategic conflict allegations [S2].

Extending mandatory gift, disclosure, and disqualification rules to all federal judges adds compliance burdens, and the bill requires a public explanation whenever any judge is disqualified, which judges argue could chill service on sensitive cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and recusal provisions address a real gap: the Supreme Court is the only part of the federal judiciary that answers to no other body for ethics violations, and the bill's disclosure rules would expose financial ties between justices and the parties before them. The main costs are administrative burdens on courts and the risk that the complaint and recusal machinery gets used strategically by litigants. On balance the bill is a substantial transparency upgrade, though its enforcement still runs largely through judges judging judges.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote for months.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill in the Senate on May 20, 2025, joined by 26 original Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced; that is the last recorded action [S4].
A total of 35 senators had signed on as cosponsors — 34 of the Senate's 45 Democrats and 1 of its 2 independents — with no Republican cosponsors [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, the rules it would have changed stay in place: justices remain the final judges of their own ethics questions, and no outside panel can review their recusal decisions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo at the Supreme Court

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court ethics bill and recruited 34 cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, Republican-controlled in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on May 20, 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican has signed on, and the chamber's 55 Republicans control the Judiciary Committee and the floor schedule.

industries.industry: Supreme Court justices and incumbent federal judges
industries.note: The bill subjects justices and judges to a binding code of conduct, complaint investigations with subpoena power, mandatory gift disclosure, and outside review of recusal decisions. Incumbent officeholders currently decide these questions for themselves.

industries.industry: High-spending court litigants and amicus filers
industries.note: Parties and outside groups filing briefs would have to disclose gifts, income, or reimbursements provided to justices and any money spent supporting a justice's confirmation, and amicus briefs would need to list major funders. These disclosures primarily affect well-funded interests whose spending now stays private.
Law firms face new disclosure duties about gifts to justices and must flag lawyer-side recusal conflicts, but firms and their clients also gain a formal process to challenge a conflicted judge.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in a Senate committee with no hearing or markup and no support from the majority party rarely advance. With no Republican cosponsors and Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and the committee chair, this bill is unlikely to move this Congress unless the political situation changes sharply.
